title: Ibn Sina: The Doctor of Doctors
summary: How Ibn Sina, born near Bukhara about a thousand years ago, became a doctor as a teenager, wrote The Canon of Medicine, and shaped how doctors in Asia and Europe worked for hundreds of years.
poll: Reading lots of books is the best way to become an expert.

versions.title: Ibn Sina: A Great Doctor
versions.text:
Ibn Sina was a great doctor. He was born long, long ago. His home was near Bukhara. That is in Uzbekistan now.

He loved to read. He learned fast. At ten, he knew the Quran by heart. He knew lots of poems, too.

As a boy, he read books on medicine. Soon he helped the sick. A sick man was his patient. Old doctors came to learn from him. He was just a teen!

One day the king got sick. No one could help. Then Ibn Sina came. He found a cure. The king got well! As a gift, he could use the king's library. It had lots of rare books.

Then he wrote a huge book. It told how to find what was wrong. It told how to help the sick. It had a long list of drugs.

He said some sickness can spread. It can pass from one man to the next. Drink clean water, he said. Eat well. Move. Sleep.

His book went far. It got to Europe. They used it there for a long time. They called him Avicenna.

He died in 1037. Now we call him the doctor of doctors.

Ibn Sina had an amazing memory, and he loved to learn. By the age of ten, he knew the Quran by heart and many poems as well. After that, he studied math, science, and logic, which is the skill of thinking clearly.

Ibn Sina believed that some diseases are contagious. This means they can spread from one person to another. He taught that clean water, good food, exercise, and sleep protect the body.

His book was later put into Latin. Doctors in Europe studied this translated book for hundreds of years. There, he was known as Avicenna.

Ibn Sina died in 1037. People still call him the doctor of doctors.

versions.title: Ibn Sina: The Doctor of Doctors
versions.text:
More than a millennium ago, around the year 980, a boy named Ibn Sina was born in the vicinity of the city of Bukhara, situated in what presently constitutes Uzbekistan. He would subsequently mature into a brilliant scholar and one of the most celebrated physicians throughout recorded history, an individual whose ideas would fundamentally shape the practice of medicine for many succeeding centuries.

Ibn Sina possessed a genuinely remarkable memory alongside an intense, almost insatiable enthusiasm for continuous learning. By merely ten years of age, he had already memorized the entire Quran and committed a considerable quantity of poetry to memory. He subsequently proceeded to study mathematics, natural science, and logic, the particular discipline concerned with reasoning clearly and systematically.

At approximately thirteen years of age, he began studying medicine entirely independently. He progressed through this material so remarkably rapidly that he was soon personally treating patients. By the time he reached sixteen, experienced, established physicians were traveling considerable distances specifically to learn directly from him.

When he was approximately seventeen years old, he was urgently summoned to the royal palace because the reigning ruler of Bukhara had fallen seriously, dangerously ill. The established royal physicians had already failed in their treatment attempts, but Ibn Sina ultimately discovered an effective cure. As his reward, he received special permission to access the extensive royal library. This library contained numerous rare manuscripts that very few individuals had ever previously enjoyed the opportunity to examine closely.

Subsequently, Ibn Sina composed The Canon of Medicine, an enormous medical encyclopedia divided systematically into five distinct books. It thoroughly explained how to properly identify the particular disease afflicting a given patient and how to treat it effectively. It additionally described hundreds of individual medicines alongside detailed instructions for their careful preparation.

Ibn Sina argued persuasively that certain diseases are inherently contagious, meaning specifically that they possess the capacity to spread readily from one person to another through various means. He also established remarkably careful, methodical rules for testing whether a particular medicine proves effective. He consistently taught that clean water, nourishing food, regular exercise, and sufficient sleep help protect the body against illness.

Medicine constituted merely one among his numerous intellectual interests, since Ibn Sina ultimately produced hundreds of additional scholarly works addressing subjects such as astronomy, music, and philosophy, including an extensive, monumental collection formally designated The Book of Healing. He frequently composed these demanding works while continuously traveling from one city to the next.

His foundational medical text was subsequently translated into Latin during the twelfth century. Physicians throughout the whole of Europe studied it diligently for several succeeding centuries, which collectively rendered it one of the most influential medical texts ever composed throughout human history. Within Europe specifically, he gradually became known under the Latinized name Avicenna.

Ibn Sina ultimately died in 1037, yet people distributed across the entire world continue honoring him today as the doctor of doctors, a fitting tribute to his enduring scholarly legacy.

versions.title: Ibn Sina: The Doctor of Doctors
versions.text:
More than a full millennium ago, around the year 980, a young boy named Ibn Sina was born in the immediate vicinity of the city of Bukhara, situated in what presently constitutes modern Uzbekistan, and he would subsequently mature into an extraordinarily brilliant scholar and one of the most celebrated physicians throughout the whole of recorded history, an individual whose original ideas would fundamentally shape the entire practice of medicine for many succeeding centuries afterward.

Ibn Sina possessed a genuinely remarkable, almost photographic memory alongside an intense, nearly insatiable enthusiasm for continuous, lifelong learning. By merely ten years of age, he had already memorized the entire Quran in its complete entirety and committed a considerable quantity of classical poetry to memory as well, and he subsequently proceeded to study mathematics, natural science, and formal logic, the particular intellectual discipline concerned specifically with reasoning clearly, rigorously, and systematically about complex problems.

At approximately thirteen years of age, he began studying medicine entirely independently and without formal instruction, and he progressed through this challenging material so remarkably rapidly that he was soon personally treating patients himself; by the time he reached merely sixteen years of age, experienced, well-established physicians were traveling considerable distances specifically to learn directly from this precocious young scholar.

When he was approximately seventeen years old, he was urgently summoned to the royal palace because the reigning ruler of Bukhara had fallen seriously and dangerously ill, with his condition worsening steadily. The established royal physicians had already failed repeatedly in their treatment attempts, but Ibn Sina ultimately succeeded in discovering an effective cure, and as his well-earned reward, he received special permission to access the extensive royal library, which contained numerous exceedingly rare manuscripts that very few individuals had ever previously enjoyed the opportunity to examine closely or study in depth.

Subsequently, Ibn Sina composed The Canon of Medicine, an enormous medical encyclopedia divided systematically into five distinct constituent books, which thoroughly explained how to properly identify the particular disease afflicting any given patient and precisely how to treat it effectively, while additionally describing hundreds of individual medicinal preparations alongside exceptionally detailed instructions for their careful compounding.

Ibn Sina argued persuasively and presciently that certain diseases are inherently contagious in nature, meaning specifically that they possess the biological capacity to spread readily from one afflicted person to another through various transmission routes. He also established remarkably careful, methodical rules for rigorously testing whether a particular medicine genuinely proves clinically effective, and he consistently taught that clean water, nourishing food, regular physical exercise, and sufficient restorative sleep collectively help protect the human body against the ongoing onset of illness and disease.

Medicine constituted merely one among his numerous wide-ranging intellectual interests, since Ibn Sina ultimately produced literally hundreds of additional scholarly works addressing subjects as varied as astronomy, music, and philosophy, including an extensive, monumental compendium formally designated The Book of Healing, even though he frequently composed these intellectually demanding works while continuously traveling from one city to the next across considerable distances.

His foundational medical text was subsequently translated carefully into Latin during the twelfth century, and physicians throughout the entirety of Europe studied it diligently and extensively for several succeeding centuries thereafter, which collectively rendered it one of the single most influential medical texts ever composed throughout the whole of human history. Within Europe specifically, he gradually became known under the Latinized name Avicenna, a designation that endures in scholarly literature even today.

Ibn Sina ultimately died in 1037, yet people distributed across the entire world continue honoring his memory today as the doctor of doctors, a thoroughly fitting tribute to his remarkably enduring scholarly legacy across the intervening centuries.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to build a library
The life of a great doctor
Why kings get sick so often
How to learn poems by heart
questions.why: The article tells about Ibn Sina's life, how he learned medicine, and how his book helped doctors for a long time.

wrong.A: A library is part of the story, but the article is about Ibn Sina.
wrong.C: Only one king gets sick in the article.
wrong.D: Learning poems is one small detail about his childhood.

questions.stem: What did Ibn Sina get after he helped the sick king?

A horse and a sword
A new name
Use of the king's library

Eat only bread
Never go outside

A person who rules a land

He went back to school.

He only knew about poems.

It was full of fun stories.

The king of Bukhara made them use it.

wrong.D: The king did not rule Europe.

wrong.C: Poetry is a small detail from his childhood.
wrong.D: The article never says he was the first to use medicine.

questions.stem: How many parts, or books, did The Canon of Medicine have?
options: Two
Ten
Five
Seventeen
questions.why: The article describes The Canon of Medicine as a giant work in five parts.

wrong.A: The article says five, not two.
wrong.B: Ten is his age when he knew the Quran by heart.
wrong.D: Seventeen is about how old he was when he cured the ruler.

questions.stem: What language was Ibn Sina's book translated into so doctors in Europe could study it?
options: Latin
Greek
Persian
French
questions.why: The article says his book was later translated into Latin.

wrong.C: Persian is not mentioned as the translation.
wrong.D: French is not mentioned.

questions.stem: Ibn Sina believed some diseases are contagious. Which situation shows a contagious disease?
options: A boy breaks his arm playing football.
A girl gets a sunburn at the beach.
A man feels tired after a long walk.
A cold spreads through a class.
questions.why: Contagious means able to spread from one person to another, like a cold spreading in a class.

wrong.A: A broken arm cannot spread to other people.
wrong.B: A sunburn does not pass from person to person.
wrong.C: Being tired after walking is not an illness that spreads.

questions.stem: Why was Ibn Sina allowed to use the royal library?
options: He paid a lot of money to the palace guards so they would let him in.
It was a reward for curing the ruler of Bukhara.
He was the ruler's son.
He worked there as a guard.
questions.why: After the palace doctors failed and Ibn Sina cured the ruler, he was given the right to use the library as his reward.

wrong.A: The article never mentions paying money.
wrong.C: He was not the ruler's son.
wrong.D: He was called to the palace as a healer, not a guard.

questions.stem: The other doctors at the palace had failed, but Ibn Sina found a cure. What can you infer from this?
options: He knew more than the older doctors.
The palace doctors did not want the ruler to get well.
The ruler was not really sick.
Ibn Sina had studied at the palace for many years.
questions.why: He succeeded where the older palace doctors could not, which shows how much he knew even as a teenager.

wrong.B: Nothing in the article suggests the doctors wanted him to stay sick.
wrong.C: The article says the ruler was very sick.
wrong.D: He was called to the palace; he had not studied there.

questions.stem: Why do you think doctors in Europe studied Ibn Sina's book for hundreds of years?
options: They could not read any other language.
It was the shortest medical book they had.
It clearly explained how to find and treat diseases.
They were required to by the ruler of Bukhara.
questions.why: The book explained how to figure out a patient's disease, how to treat it, and hundreds of medicines, so it stayed useful for a long time.

wrong.A: The book had to be translated for them, so this is not the reason.
wrong.B: The article calls it a giant work, not a short one.
wrong.D: The ruler of Bukhara did not rule Europe.

questions.stem: Why does the author include details about Ibn Sina's childhood, such as knowing the Quran by heart at age ten?
options: To explain the history of Bukhara
To show his strong memory and love of learning from an early age
To compare him with other children of his time
To give steps for memorizing long texts
questions.why: These details show readers how quickly and eagerly he learned, which helps explain how he became a great physician so young.

wrong.A: The article gives almost no history of Bukhara.
wrong.D: The article gives no steps for memorizing.

MID.prompt: Explain how Ibn Sina's ideas could still help people stay healthy today. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained at least one of Ibn Sina's ideas about health.
I used at least two details from the article.
I connected his ideas to life today.
MID.modelAnswer: Ibn Sina's idea that some diseases are contagious still helps people stay healthy today, because we now know to stay away from sick people so an illness does not spread. He also taught that clean water, good food, exercise, and sleep help protect the body, and physicians still give this same advice to patients today. These two simple ideas are still part of how doctors think about staying healthy.

keyWords.definition: a person who has studied a subject deeply and knows a great deal about it
keyWords.example: The scholar spent years studying old maps of Arabia.

keyWords.definition: a large book or set of books with information about many topics
keyWords.example: I looked up volcanoes in the encyclopedia for my report.

keyWords.definition: able to spread from one person to another
keyWords.example: Doctors asked people with the contagious illness to stay home.

keyWords.definition: changed from one language into another
keyWords.example: The story was translated from Arabic into ten languages.

keyWords.definition: having a strong effect on how people think or act
keyWords.example: Her influential speech made many students start recycling.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Ibn Sina was a gifted scholar whose medical writing shaped medicine for centuries.
Ibn Sina became famous mainly because he traveled to many cities.
Ibn Sina cared far more about music, astronomy, and philosophy than about treating patients.
Ibn Sina's ideas were forgotten soon after he died.
questions.why: The article traces his early learning, his medical encyclopedia, and how influential it became in Europe for hundreds of years.

wrong.B: Travel is a minor detail; his fame came from his knowledge and writing.
wrong.C: The article calls medicine his main field and other subjects additional interests.
wrong.D: The article says his book was studied for hundreds of years and he is still honored.

questions.stem: According to the article, which contribution did Ibn Sina make besides describing diseases and treatments?
options: He built the first hospital in Bukhara.
He set out careful rules for testing whether a medicine really works.
He invented a printing press so that medical books could be copied quickly.
He translated his own book into Latin.
questions.why: The article states that he set out careful rules for testing whether a medicine genuinely works.

wrong.A: The article does not mention him building a hospital.
wrong.C: The printing press is not mentioned.
wrong.D: His book was translated in the twelfth century, long after his death.

questions.stem: When was The Canon of Medicine translated into Latin?
options: In the twelfth century
When Ibn Sina was seventeen
In the year 980
In the year 1037
questions.why: The article says it was translated into Latin in the twelfth century.

wrong.B: At seventeen he cured the ruler; the book did not exist yet.
wrong.C: 980 is around when he was born.
wrong.D: 1037 is the year he died.

questions.stem: The article calls The Canon of Medicine one of the most influential medical texts ever written. What does influential mean in this sentence?
options: Very long and difficult to read
Written in many languages at once
Strongly shaping what people thought
Kept secret by a small group
questions.why: Doctors studied it for hundreds of years, so it strongly shaped how medicine was practiced.

wrong.A: Length and difficulty are not what influential means.
wrong.B: It was translated, but influential does not mean multilingual.
wrong.D: The book was widely studied, not kept secret.

questions.stem: What can you infer from the fact that Ibn Sina often wrote while traveling from city to city?
options: He did not take his writing seriously.
He was determined to keep writing even in difficult conditions.
He wrote only short notes while traveling.
He traveled because no city would accept him.
questions.why: Writing hundreds of works while often on the move shows strong commitment and focus.

wrong.A: Producing hundreds of works shows the opposite.
wrong.C: The article mentions a vast collection, not just short notes.
wrong.D: The article gives no reason like this for his travels.

questions.stem: How did gaining access to the royal library most likely affect Ibn Sina's later work?
options: It made him lose interest in medicine.
It let him learn from rare books.
It forced him to stop treating patients.
It made him the ruler of Bukhara.
questions.why: The library held rare books few people had read, which would have deepened the knowledge he later gathered in his encyclopedia.

wrong.A: He went on to write a huge medical encyclopedia.
wrong.C: The article does not say he stopped treating patients.
wrong.D: Using the library did not make him a ruler.

questions.stem: How is Ibn Sina's experience as a teenager different from that of most young students today?
options: He studied medicine mostly on his own and was treating patients by sixteen.
He went to medical school for many years before seeing patients.
He studied only one subject his whole life.
He learned medicine by watching the palace doctors.
questions.why: The article says he studied medicine independently and was treating patients so early that older physicians came to learn from him.

wrong.B: The article says he studied largely on his own, not in a long formal program.
wrong.C: He studied mathematics, science, logic, and later many other subjects.
wrong.D: The palace doctors failed to cure the ruler; he did not learn from them.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the paragraph about astronomy, music, philosophy, and The Book of Healing?
options: To show that medicine was a small part of his life
To show that his knowledge reached far beyond medicine
To explain how The Book of Healing cured the ruler
To argue that music is more important than medicine
questions.why: The paragraph shows the wide range of subjects he studied and wrote about, which supports calling him a brilliant scholar.

wrong.A: The article makes medicine the center of his fame.
wrong.C: The ruler was cured long before; The Book of Healing was not a cure.
wrong.D: The author makes no such argument.

HIGH.prompt: The article says Ibn Sina's ideas shaped medicine for centuries. Explain which of his ideas you think was most important and why, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I named one of Ibn Sina's ideas or contributions.
I explained why I think it was important.
I supported my explanation with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think Ibn Sina's idea that diseases can be contagious was his most important contribution, because it changed how people understood the spread of illness centuries before germs were discovered. The article explains that he recognized some diseases could pass from person to person, an insight that later scholars and physicians built upon as they developed ways to prevent outbreaks. His comprehensive book, The Canon of Medicine, worked almost like an encyclopedia of disease and treatment, and it was later translated into Latin so European doctors could study his contagious-disease theory for hundreds of years. Because this one influential idea shaped medical thinking across cultures and centuries, I believe it was Ibn Sina's single most important contribution to medicine.
